before.query: select id, court_id, member_id, start_time, end_time, status from health.bookings where club_id = $1 and start_time >= $2 and start_time < $3 order by start_time

after.query: select id, court_id, member_id, start_time, end_time, status from health.bookings where club_id = $1 and start_time >= $2 and start_time < $3 order by start_time

auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.explanation: The bookings_own policy decides which bookings a signed-in player can see by calling auth.uid(), which returns the ID of the logged-in user. Written as it is, Postgres re-runs that check for every booking row instead of once per query, which slows down reads as the bookings table grows. Wrapping the call in a subquery, (select auth.uid()), lets Postgres evaluate it once, and the access rule itself stays the same: players see only their own bookings.
auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.impact: Players loading their booking lists and any query touching health.bookings under RLS will get faster as data grows; access rights do not change.
auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.fix_summary: Recreate the bookings_own SELECT policy so auth.uid() is wrapped in a subquery, keeping the same own-bookings rule, inside a single transaction.
auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.draft_sql: BEGIN; DROP POLICY IF EXISTS bookings_own ON health.bookings; CREATE POLICY bookings_own ON health.bookings AS PERMISSIVE FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (member_id IN (SELECT m.id FROM health.members m WHERE m.user_id = (select auth.uid()))); COMMIT;
auth_rls_initplan:bookings:bookings_own.rollback_sql: BEGIN; DROP POLICY IF EXISTS bookings_own ON health.bookings; CREATE POLICY bookings_own ON health.bookings AS PERMISSIVE FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (member_id IN (SELECT m.id FROM health.members m WHERE m.user_id = auth.uid())); COMMIT;

duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.explanation: Two indexes on health.members cover the same column (user_id), so the database keeps and updates two identical copies of the same lookup structure. This wastes storage and slows down every insert and update to members, because each write must maintain both copies, even though one copy is enough to serve queries that filter on user_id.
duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.impact: Club staff and players see no change in results, but writes to the members table do redundant index work and the table uses extra storage; the members_self row-level security policy on user_id still benefits from one remaining index.
duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.fix_summary: Drop the redundant index members_user_idx and keep members_user_id_idx, which covers the same column and follows the naming pattern.
duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.draft_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.members_user_idx;
duplicate_index:members:members_user_id_.rollback_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS members_user_idx ON health.members USING btree (user_id);

function_search_path_mutable:is_staff:is.explanation: The is_staff function checks whether the current user is staff at a given club, and it runs with the owner's privileges (SECURITY DEFINER). It does not pin the search_path, which is the list of schemas Postgres searches when resolving names, so a user who can create objects in an earlier schema could in principle redirect those lookups to their own objects. Pinning the search_path closes that gap without changing what the function does, since its body already uses fully qualified names.
function_search_path_mutable:is_staff:is.impact: Club staff permission checks that rely on this function are affected, and the security risk is that a privileged function could resolve names to attacker-controlled objects; normal player bookings are not changed by this fix.
function_search_path_mutable:is_staff:is.fix_summary: Set a fixed, empty search_path on health.is_staff(uuid) so that its names resolve only through the fully qualified references in its body.
function_search_path_mutable:is_staff:is.draft_sql: ALTER FUNCTION health.is_staff(p_club uuid) SET search_path = '';
function_search_path_mutable:is_staff:is.rollback_sql: ALTER FUNCTION health.is_staff(p_club uuid) RESET search_path;

permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.explanation: The payments table has a policy named payments_all that allows any signed-in user to read every row, because its condition is simply true. Courtline's rule is that a player sees only their own payments, and staff see payments for their club, so this policy exposes other members' financial records.
permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.impact: Every signed-in player and any account on the app can read all payments across all clubs, including amounts, statuses and member IDs, which is a serious privacy and security exposure for members and club staff.
permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.fix_summary: Replace the permissive payments_all SELECT policy with one that allows a row only when its member belongs to the signed-in user or the signed-in user is staff of the row's club.
permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.draft_sql: DROP POLICY IF EXISTS payments_all ON health.payments; CREATE POLICY payments_own_or_staff ON health.payments FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (member_id IN (SELECT m.id FROM health.members m WHERE m.user_id = (SELECT auth.uid())) OR health.is_staff(club_id));
permissive_policy:payments:payments_all.rollback_sql: DROP POLICY IF EXISTS payments_own_or_staff ON health.payments; CREATE POLICY payments_all ON health.payments FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (true);

rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.explanation: The leagues table is reachable through the API, but row level security (Postgres's per-row access check) is switched off, so any signed-in user can read every league at every club. Courtline's rule is that league data should be visible only to members of the club that owns it.
rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.impact: Players at other clubs can see league names and levels they should not have access to, and this is a data exposure that club staff and players would both care about.
rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.fix_summary: Enable row level security on health.leagues and add a SELECT policy that only returns rows where health.is_member(club_id) is true.
rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.draft_sql: ALTER TABLE health.leagues ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY leagues_select_club_members ON health.leagues FOR SELECT USING (health.is_member(club_id));
rls_disabled_in_exposed_schema:leagues:l.rollback_sql: DROP POLICY IF EXISTS leagues_select_club_members ON health.leagues; ALTER TABLE health.leagues DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

rls_enabled_no_policy:lesson_notes:lesso.explanation: Row Level Security (RLS, Postgres's per-row access control) is turned on for the lesson_notes table, but it has no policies, so the database blocks every API user from reading any row. Courtline's access rule is that only club staff should see these lesson notes, and the current setup hides them from everyone, including staff.
rls_enabled_no_policy:lesson_notes:lesso.impact: Club staff cannot read lesson notes through the API, and no other user can either, so the feature does not work for the people it is meant for.
rls_enabled_no_policy:lesson_notes:lesso.fix_summary: Add a SELECT policy on health.lesson_notes that lets a signed-in user read a row only when health.is_staff(club_id) returns true for that row's club.
rls_enabled_no_policy:lesson_notes:lesso.draft_sql: CREATE POLICY lesson_notes_staff_select ON health.lesson_notes FOR SELECT USING (health.is_staff(club_id));
rls_enabled_no_policy:lesson_notes:lesso.rollback_sql: DROP POLICY IF EXISTS lesson_notes_staff_select ON health.lesson_notes;

unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.explanation: Bookings have a foreign key (a link guaranteeing each booking's club_id matches a real club) but no index on club_id. Without an index, Postgres must scan the whole bookings table to find a club's bookings, for example when filtering by club or checking a club before it is deleted. This is a performance issue, not a data-integrity one.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.impact: Club staff and any queries filtering bookings by club may run slower as the bookings table grows, and deleting or changing a club row has to scan bookings; players' data and access rules are not affected.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.fix_summary: Add a btree index on health.bookings(club_id) so lookups and foreign key checks by club can use the index.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.draft_sql: CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS bookings_club_id_idx ON health.bookings (club_id);

unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.explanation: The bookings table has a foreign key bookings_court_id_fkey linking court_id to a court, but no index starts with court_id. Postgres does not create that index automatically, so lookups and deletes that filter or check by court_id, such as finding all bookings for a court or removing a court, must scan the whole bookings table. This is a performance issue rather than a correctness one, and it grows with the number of bookings.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.impact: Club staff and players may see slower court schedules and booking lookups as bookings accumulate, and deleting or changing courts can become slow because Postgres scans bookings to check the foreign key.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.fix_summary: Create a btree index on health.bookings(court_id) so the foreign key is covered, built concurrently to avoid blocking writes.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.draft_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS bookings_court_id_idx ON health.bookings USING btree (court_id);
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.rollback_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.bookings_court_id_idx;

unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.explanation: The bookings table has a foreign key (a link to the members table through member_id) with no index on member_id, so Postgres has to scan every booking row whenever it checks or looks up bookings by member. The bookings_own row-level security policy filters bookings by member_id on every authenticated read, so this unindexed column sits on the hot path for member booking queries.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.impact: Members viewing their own bookings and any operation that changes or deletes a member row (which checks bookings referencing it) may run slower as the bookings table grows.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.fix_summary: Add a non-unique b-tree index on health.bookings(member_id), built concurrently so writes are not blocked during creation.
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.draft_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS bookings_member_id_idx ON health.bookings USING btree (member_id);
unindexed_foreign_keys:bookings:bookings.rollback_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.bookings_member_id_idx;

slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.explanation: Courtline's bookings table has 200,000 rows, and the schedule query filters on club_id and a start_time range, but the only index is on id. Postgres therefore reads every row to find the matching bookings, which averages 6.741 ms per run and adds up to 808.9 ms across 120 runs. A composite index on (club_id, start_time) lets Postgres jump straight to one club's bookings in the requested time window and return them already sorted.
slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.impact: Club staff and players loading court schedules see slower responses, and the database does unnecessary work on every schedule view.
slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.fix_summary: Add a concurrent composite index on health.bookings (club_id, start_time) so the club and time-range lookup no longer scans the whole table.
slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.draft_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS bookings_club_id_start_time_idx ON health.bookings (club_id, start_time);
slow_query:bookings:club_id+start_time.rollback_sql: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS health.bookings_club_id_start_time_idx;

judge.reason: The facts do not identify the auth function as auth.uid() or establish that the policy lets players see only their own bookings.
The facts do not specify the indexed column, and not every update necessarily maintains both indexes.
The claim that the function body already uses fully qualified names is not supported by the facts.
The exposure is described clearly, but the facts do not establish that staff access under own_or_staff is limited to their club.
The explanation invents a rule restricting league visibility to members of the owning club.
The facts establish that API users cannot read the notes, but not that Courtline intends access to be staff-only.
It clearly explains the missing index and the likely performance consequences without implying that data integrity is broken.
It plainly explains why the missing index can make court-related lookups and foreign-key checks slower.
The facts do not establish that the bookings_own policy filters by member_id on every authenticated read.
It invents that the only index is on id and promises sorted results without a stated sort order.
